claims.evidence: This is supported by the heat map analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, with speculation about the biological meaning.

claims.claim: Sth1 peaks are most abundant in the NDRs, where CUT&RUN profiles show a gradual increase in yield with digestion times between 5 s and 10 min, indicating that quantitative limit digestions are obtained.
claims.source: Sth1 peaks are most abundant in the NDRs, where CUT&RUN profiles show a gradual increase in yield with digestion times between 5 s and 10 min (Figure 4B), indicating that quantitative limit digestions are obtained using our protocol.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the Sth1 time-course data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: A nearly flat line was observed for the negative control derived from 3XFLAG-Sth1 nuclei treated in parallel for the maximum digestion time, but where the primary anti-FLAG antibody was omitted.
claims.source: Importantly, we observed a nearly flat line for our negative control derived from 3XFLAG-Sth1 nuclei treated in parallel for the maximum digestion time, but where the primary anti-FLAG antibody was omitted.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the negative control data shown in Figure 4B demonstrating specificity.

claims.claim: Results for Sth1 CUT&RUN are similar to results for Sth1 ORGANIC profiling, but with much higher yield.
claims.source: Our results for Sth1 CUT&RUN are similar to results for Sth1 ORGANIC profiling (Ramachandran et al., 2015), but with much higher yield (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison of Sth1 CUT&RUN and ORGANIC data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: CUT&RUN provides efficient high-resolution mapping of chromatin-associated complexes, even those that are very large and dynamic.
claims.source: We conclude that CUT&RUN provides efficient high-resolution mapping of chromatin-associated complexes, even those that are very large and dynamic.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is supported by the successful mapping of Mot1 and Sth1, which are large dynamic complexes.

claims.claim: There is only one centromeric nucleosome per chromosome in budding yeast, which is only ~1% the molar abundance of Abf1 or Reb1.
claims.source: In budding yeast, there is only only one centromeric nucleosome per chromosome, which is only ~1% the molar abundance of Abf1 or Reb1.
claims.evidence: This is based on known biology of yeast centromeres.

claims.claim: The centromeric nucleosome contains the CenH3 (Cse4) histone variant in place of H3.
claims.source: An additional challenge to studying the centromeric nucleosome, which contains the CenH3 (Cse4) histone variant in place of H3, is that it is part of the multi-megadalton kinetochore complex throughout the cell cycle (Akiyoshi et al., 2010), which renders it highly insoluble (Krassovsky et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies on centromeric chromatin structure.

claims.claim: The centromeric nucleosome is part of the multi-megadalton kinetochore complex throughout the cell cycle, which renders it highly insoluble.
claims.source: An additional challenge to studying the centromeric nucleosome, which contains the CenH3 (Cse4) histone variant in place of H3, is that it is part of the multi-megadalton kinetochore complex throughout the cell cycle (Akiyoshi et al., 2010), which renders it highly insoluble (Krassovsky et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies on kinetochore structure and solubility.

claims.claim: The highest Cse4 occupancy on the chromosome is seen at the centromere for the insoluble kinetochore.
claims.source: As expected for the insoluble kinetochore, the highest Cse4 occupancy on the chromosome is seen at the centromere (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the Cse4 occupancy data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Occupancy of insoluble H2A, which is present in every nucleosome throughout the genome, is also maximum at the centromere.
claims.source: Strikingly, occupancy of insoluble H2A, which is present in every nucleosome througout the genome, is also maximum at the centromere.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the H2A occupancy data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: At all 16 yeast centromeres, very similar enrichments of Cse4 and H2A were observed confined to the ~120 bp functional centromere over the digestion time-course, with resolution that is 4-fold better than that of standard X-ChIP.
claims.source: Indeed, at all 16 yeast centromeres we observe very similar enrichments of Cse4 and H2A confined to the ~120 bp functional centromere over the digestion time-course, with resolution that is 4-fold better than that of standard X-ChIP (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the centromere alignment data shown in Figure 5B and comparison to X-ChIP.

claims.claim: Crosslinking results in a more distinct profile and the appearance of phased nucleosomes on either side of the centromere, which is interpreted as a reduction in chromatin flexibility with crosslinking.
claims.source: Interestingly, crosslinking results in a more distinct profile and the appearance of phased nucleosomes on either side, which we interpret as a reduction in chromatin flexiblity with crosslinking, while demonstrating that the basic strategy can be applied to crosslinked cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the crosslinked CUT&RUN data shown in Figure 5D, with interpretation of the biological meaning.

claims.claim: The unequivocal presence of insoluble H2A in the centromeric nucleosome directly addresses the continuing controversy over its composition.
claims.source: The unequivocal presence of insoluble H2A in the centromeric nucleosome directly addresses the continuing controversy over its composition (Wisniewski et al., 2014; Henikoff et al., 2014; Aravamudhan et al., 2013; Shivaraju et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the H2A data at centromeres and citations to publications debating centromere composition.

claims.claim: The intactness of the centromeric particle over a >100 fold digestion time-course demonstrates that CUT&RUN is not biased by the inherent preference of MNase for AT-rich DNA.
claims.source: Moreover, as the yeast centromeric nucleosome wraps DNA that is >90% A+T (Krassovsky et al., 2012), the intactness of the centromeric particle over a >100 fold digestion time-course (Figure 5) demonstrates that CUT&RUN is not biased by the inherent preference of MNase for AT-rich DNA (Chung et al., 2010; McGhee and Felsenfeld, 1983).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the centromere data and citations regarding MNase sequence bias and centromere composition.

claims.claim: CUT&RUN can map large DNA-binding complexes, even those that are rare, insoluble and AT-rich.
claims.source: We conclude that CUT&RUN can map large DNA-binding complexes, even those that are rare, insoluble and AT-rich.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is supported by the successful mapping of the rare, insoluble, AT-rich centromeric nucleosome.

claims.claim: Examination of the ≥150 bp profiles reveals broad peaks around the binding sites, sometimes with 'notches' corresponding to the sites themselves that deepen with time of digestion.
claims.source: Examination of the ≥150 bp profiles (Figure 1D and Figure 4) reveals broad peaks around the binding sites, sometimes with 'notches' corresponding to the sites themselves that deepen with time of digestion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the ≥150 bp fragment profiles shown in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: The broad peak pattern is interpreted as representing the gradual release of fragments with one end resulting from cleavage around the TF-DNA complex and a second cleavage that is close enough to the TF-bound site to produce a soluble fragment.
claims.source: We interpret this pattern as representing the gradual release of fragments with one end resulting from cleavage around the TF-DNA complex and a second cleavage that is close enough to the TF-bound site to produce a soluble fragment.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed ≥150 bp fragment patterns.

claims.claim: Heat map analysis of the ≥150 bp fragments showed occupancy of Abf1 and Reb1 fragments over their respective binding motifs, extending ~0.5 kb on either side.
claims.source: Heat map analysis of the ≥150 bp fragments also showed occupancy of Abf1 and Reb1 fragments over their respective binding motifs, extending ~0.5 kb on either side (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the heat map analysis shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Extended local cleavage is reminiscent of the >1 kb reach of DamID, suggesting that the flexibility of the tether results in probing of nearby chromatin.
claims.source: Such extended local cleavage is reminiscent of the >1 kb reach of DamID (van Steensel et al., 2001), which suggests that the flexibility of the tether results in probing of nearby chromatin.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison to DamID and the observed extended cleavage patterns.

claims.claim: CTCF CUT&RUN showed higher dynamic range than other profiling methods, including standard X-ChIP-seq and ChIP-exo, when comparing 10 million randomly selected reads.
claims.source: To directly compare the efficiency of various methods, we randomly selected 10 million reads for each technique and plotted the raw scores as an indication of information content per sequenced read. As was the case for yeast TFs, CTCF CUT&RUN showed higher dynamic range than other profiling methods, including standard X-ChIP-seq and ChIP-exo (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison of CTCF profiling methods shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: When aligned to CTCF motifs found within DNaseI hypersensitive sites or previously identified binding sites, CUT&RUN and X-ChIP-seq CTCF heat maps showed strong concordance, with CUT&RUN having a higher dynamic range.
claims.source: When aligned to CTCF motifs found within DNaseI hypersensitive sites or previously identified binding sites, CUT&RUN and X-ChIP-seq CTCF heat maps showed strong concordance, with CUT&RUN having a higher dynamic range (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the heat map comparison shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: A no antibody control showed undetectable background when CUT&RUN is performed at low temperature.
claims.source: A no antibody control showed undetectable background (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) when CUT&RUN is performed at low temperature (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the negative control data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: CUT&RUN releases neighboring fragments corresponding to phased nucleosomes immediately adjacent to CTCF sites.
claims.source: As was the case for budding yeast TFs, we observed release of the neighboring fragments, which correspond to phased nucleosomes immediately adjacent to CTCF sites.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the ≥150 bp fragment data showing nucleosome-sized fragments flanking CTCF sites.

claims.claim: Pronounced 'tram-tracks' separated by 44 bp at defined positions relative to the CTCF motif were observed by plotting just the end positions of the short CUT&RUN fragments.
claims.source: By plotting just the end positions of the short CUT&RUN fragments that are the cleavage positions of the tethered MNase, we observed pronounced 'tram-tracks' separated by 44 bp at defined positions relative to the CTCF motif.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the fragment end position analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The exact cleavage pattern is consistent over a ~300 fold time-course digestion range, with a predominant single base-pair cut site on either side of the CTCF-bound site, highlighting the limit digest obtained.
claims.source: Furthermore, the exact cleavage pattern is consistent over a ~300 fold time-course digestion range, with a predominant single base-pair cut site on either side of the CTCF-bound site, highlighting the limit digest obtained (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the time-course cleavage pattern data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The cleavage pattern indicates that the cleavage positions are precise and highly homogeneous within the population of cells.
claims.source: This pattern indicates that the cleavage positions are precise and highly homogeneous within the population of cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the consistent cleavage patterns observed across the cell population.

claims.claim: CUT&RUN accurately maps both the TFs and their flanking chromatin in the same experiment.
claims.source: Our results suggest that CUT&RUN accurately maps both the TFs and their flanking chromatin in the same experiment.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the observation of both TF footprints and flanking nucleosomes in the same dataset.

claims.claim: CUT&RUN successfully mapped both Myc and Max at high resolution.
claims.source: We therefore tested CUT&RUN using Myc and Max which are basic-loop-helix proteins that bind to a short E-box motif and have b residence times (Phair et al., 2004). CUT&RUN successfully mapped both Myc and Max at high resolution (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the Myc and Max mapping data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: For Max, CUT&RUN had a much higher dynamic range than ENCODE ChIP-seq and was able to robustly identify a much larger number of Max binding sites.
claims.source: In the case of Max, a quantitative comparison with ENCODE ChIP-seq data is possible as the same antibody was used, and here CUT&RUN had a much higher dynamic range and therefore was able to robustly identify a much larger number of Max binding sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison of Max CUT&RUN and ENCODE ChIP-seq shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: Max is present at almost all Myc binding sites, as expected since Myc forms a heterodimer with Max to bind DNA at E-boxes.
claims.source: To bind DNA at E-boxes, Myc forms a heterodimer with Max (Blackwood et al., 1991) but in addition Max has other binding partners (Ayer and Eisenman, 1993), As expected, we see very high overlap with Max present at almost all Myc binding sites.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the overlap analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B and citations to studies on Myc-Max heterodimerization.

claims.claim: There is poor overlap between previously identified binding sites by ENCODE X-ChIP-seq for Myc and Max, as 10-fold fewer Max sites were identified.
claims.source: In contrast, there is poor overlap between previously identified binding sites by ENCODE X-ChIP-seq for Myc and Max, as 10-fold fewer Max sites were identified.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison of ENCODE peak calls shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: When Max ENCODE X-ChIP-seq data were lined up over Max CUT&RUN sites, high occupancy was observed, suggesting that the lower dynamic range of X-ChIP-seq relative to CUT&RUN was responsible for the failure to identify these Max binding sites by X-ChIP-seq.
claims.source: However, when we lined up Max ENCODE X-ChIP-seq data over Max CUT&RUN sites, we saw high occupancy (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C), suggesting that the lower dynamic range of X-ChIP-seq relative to CUT&RUN was responsible for the failure to identify these Max binding sites by X-ChIP-seq.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the heat map analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3C.

claims.claim: By analyzing 10 million reads from CUT&RUN and ENCODE X-ChIP-seq, similar H3K27me3 landscapes were observed, but at a much higher dynamic range for CUT&RUN.
claims.source: By analyzing 10 million reads from CUT&RUN and ENCODE X-ChIP-seq, we observed similar H3K27me3 landscapes, but at a much higher dynamic range for CUT&RUN, which demonstrates that Protein A-MNase is able to access compacted chromatin (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the H3K27me3 comparison shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Protein A-MNase is able to access compacted chromatin.
claims.source: By analyzing 10 million reads from CUT&RUN and ENCODE X-ChIP-seq, we observed similar H3K27me3 landscapes, but at a much higher dynamic range for CUT&RUN, which demonstrates that Protein A-MNase is able to access compacted chromatin (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the successful mapping of H3K27me3, a mark associated with compacted heterochromatin.

claims.claim: H3K27me3 cleaved chromatin is readily released from the intact nuclei into the soluble fraction, indicating that CUT&RUN is applicable to probing protein-DNA interactions in compacted chromatin.
claims.source: Furthermore, H3K27me3 cleaved chromatin is readily released from the intact nuclei into the soluble fraction, indicating that CUT&RUN is applicable to probing protein-DNA interactions in compacted chromatin.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the H3K27me3 data showing release of fragments into the soluble fraction.

claims.claim: Native ChIP mapping of CTCF identified 2298 sites with high motif scores.
claims.source: We developed a new native ChIP protocol (Appendix 1), and achieved near-complete protein extraction with no evidence of protein redistribution (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). Under native conditions, we identified 2298 sites with high motif scores.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the native ChIP data and peak calling results.

claims.claim: CUT&RUN mapping of CTCF detected ~22,000 sites that were also present in X-ChIP, with a diverse range of motif scores.
claims.source: In contrast, CUT&RUN mapping of CTCF detected ~22,000 sites that were also present in X-ChIP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), with a diverse range of motif scores (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the CUT&RUN peak calling and motif score analysis.

claims.claim: All sites identified by native ChIP were robustly detected by CUT&RUN and X-ChIP, showing a similar signal distribution.
claims.source: As expected, all sites identified by native ChIP also were robustly detected by CUT&RUN and X-ChIP, showing a similar signal distribution (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: CUT&RUN sites lacking a significant native ChIP signal nevertheless showed a robust footprint in the native ChIP input with a similar cumulative distribution of counts, indicating the presence of unknown bound factors.
claims.source: CUT&RUN sites lacking a significant native ChIP signal nevertheless showed a robust footprint in the native ChIP input with a similar cumulative distribution of counts (Figure 7B), indicating the presence of unknown bound factors, as would be expected for 3D genomic interactions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7B, with inference about 3D interactions.

claims.claim: CUT&RUN, as with X-ChIP, can discover both direct (native CTCF peak) and indirect (CUT&RUN peak only) chromatin interactions at high resolution.
claims.source: This suggests that CUT&RUN, as with X-ChIP, can discover both direct (native CTCF peak) and indirect (CUT&RUN peak only) chromatin interactions at high resolution.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of native ChIP and CUT&RUN peak calls.

claims.claim: For a typical ~1 Mb genomic region, all high-scoring ChIA-PET fragments overlap with direct and indirect sites.
claims.source: We find that for a typical ~1 Mb genomic region all high-scoring ChIA-PET fragments overlap with direct and indirect sites (Figure 8A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the ChIA-PET overlap analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: 91% of the direct sites are present in CTCF ChIA-PET data, with 43% of these ChIA-PET fragments interacting with an indirect site.
claims.source: Moreover, 91% of the direct sites are present in CTCF ChIA-PET data, with 43% of these ChIA-PET fragments interacting with an indirect site, and the remainder contained a high CUT&RUN signal (Figure 8C), which suggests these are indirect sites involved in multiple contacts, just below the peak calling threshold.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the ChIA-PET interaction analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: A high frequency of Hi-C interactions between direct sites and indirect sites was found, with a quantitative correlation between Hi-C score and CUT&RUN signal at the indirect sites.
claims.source: As further evidence that CUT&RUN can detect indirect contact interactions, we found a high frequency of Hi-C interactions between direct sites and indirect sites and a quantitative correlation between Hi-C score and CUT&RUN signal at the indirect sites (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the Hi-C correlation analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: By comparing CUT&RUN and native ChIP it is possible to map contact sites at near base-pair resolution, to distinguish direct from indirect protein binding sites that result from long-range genomic interactions, and to determine the directionality to these contacts.
claims.source: Therefore, by comparing CUT&RUN and native ChIP it is possible to map contact sites at near base-pair resolution, to distinguish direct from indirect protein binding sites that result from long-range genomic interactions, and to determine the directionality to these contacts, not feasible by other methods.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined analysis of CUT&RUN, native ChIP, ChIA-PET, and Hi-C data.

claims.claim: When normalized to spike-in DNA, the number of cleavage events is proportional to the starting cell number.
claims.source: When normalized to spike-in DNA, we observed that the number of cleavage events is proportional to the starting cell number (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the cell titration experiment shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: When the data are normalized to the total number of reads aligning to the human genome, there is no clear difference in the samples, suggesting that high data quality is maintained with low input material.
claims.source: Furthermore, when the data are normalized to the total number of reads aligning to the human genome, there is no clear difference in the samples, suggesting that high data quality is maintained with low input material.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison of standard normalization across different cell numbers shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: CUT&RUN performs as well as or better than ChIP-seq with respect to simplicity, resolution, robustness, efficiency, data quality, and applicability to highly insoluble complexes.
claims.source: We find that CUT&RUN performs as well as or better than ChIP-seq with respect to simplicity, resolution, robustness, efficiency, data quality, and applicability to highly insoluble complexes.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the comparative data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: CUT&RUN requires only ~1/10th of the sequencing depth of other high resolution methodologies due to the intrinsically low background achieved by performing the reaction in situ.
claims.source: CUT&RUN requires only ~1/10th of the sequencing depth of other high resolution methodologies due to the intrinsically low background achieved by performing the reaction in situ.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparative sequencing depth requirements shown throughout the results.

claims.claim: CUT&RUN can probe the local environment around the targeted site because nuclei are intact when MNase is activated.
claims.source: As nuclei are intact when MNase is activated, CUT&RUN can probe the local environment around the targeted site.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the observation of flanking nucleosomes and extended cleavage patterns.

claims.claim: CUT&RUN recovers sites of 3D contacts with base-pair resolution at relatively low sequencing depth in human cells.
claims.source: Indeed, we find that CUT&RUN recovers sites of 3D contacts with base-pair resolution at relatively low sequencing depth in human cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the CTCF contact site mapping data.

claims.claim: CUT&RUN is antibody-based, so that it can be applied to any epitope on chromatin, making it a general method for chromatin profiling.
claims.source: Like ChIP, CUT&RUN is antibody-based, so that it can be applied to any epitope on chromatin, making it a general method for chromatin profiling that takes advantage of the large antibody production infrastructure developed for ChIP.
claims.evidence: This is based on the antibody-based design of CUT&RUN and the demonstration with multiple different targets.

claims.claim: CUT&RUN provides quantitative occupancy profiles with standard and spike-in normalization options.
claims.source: CUT&RUN provides quantitative occupancy profiles with standard and spike-in normalization options implemented by our custom software for processing and comparing ChIP-seq and CUT&RUN datasets.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the normalization methods described and demonstrated in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The only non-standard feature of CUT&RUN is the requirement for the pA-MN fusion protein, which can be produced and purified in a batch from bacterial culture that yields enough pA-MN for profiling >100,000 samples.
claims.source: The only non-standard feature of CUT&RUN is the requirement for the pA-MN fusion protein, which can be produced and purified in a batch from bacterial culture that yields enough pA-MN for profiling >100,000 samples.
claims.evidence: This is based on the protocol for pA-MN production and the amounts required per reaction.

claims.claim: CUT&RUN can resolve crosslinking-, sonication- and solubilization-related issues because it is based on different principles from ChIP.
claims.source: As CUT&RUN is based on different principles from ChIP, it can resolve crosslinking-, sonication- and solubilization-related issues.
claims.evidence: This is based on the in situ nature of CUT&RUN and the absence of these steps in the protocol.

claims.claim: Backgrounds are low with CUT&RUN because cleavages occur only around binding sites, whereas ChIP first pulverizes the entire genome.
claims.source: Backgrounds are low with CUT&RUN, because cleavages occur only around binding sites, whereas ChIP first pulverizes the entire genome, and these fragments contribute to a genome-wide background noise that must still be sequenced.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation for the observed low background in CUT&RUN.

claims.claim: The near absence of detectable background under brief low-temperature conditions, the lack of preference for accessible or AT-rich DNA, and the recovery of essentially all Abf1 and Reb1 motifs in the yeast genome suggest that CUT&RUN is not subject to the types of artifacts that sometimes have plagued ChIP.
claims.source: The near absence of detectable background under the brief low-temperature conditions that we used, the lack of preference for accessible or AT-rich DNA, and the recovery of essentially all Abf1 and Reb1 motifs in the yeast genome, suggests that CUT&RUN is not subject to the types of artifacts that sometimes have plagued ChIP (Teytelman et al., 2013; Park et al., 2013; Jain et al., 2015; Baranello et al., 2016; Kasinathan et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and citations to studies documenting ChIP artifacts.

claims.claim: CUT&RUN antibody binding takes place in an intact nuclear environment resembling conditions for immunofluorescence microscopy, so that it should be successful for antibodies that are validated cytologically, even those that fail in ChIP.
claims.source: Furthermore, CUT&RUN antibody binding takes place in an intact nuclear environment resembling conditions for immunofluorescence microscopy, so that it should be successful for antibodies that are validated cytologically, even those that fail in ChIP.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the in situ nature of antibody binding in CUT&RUN.

claims.claim: CUT&RUN should be appropriate for extending classical chromatin salt-fractionation to specific TFs and chromatin complexes because it solubilizes chromatin only after the targeted cleavage reaction.
claims.source: As CUT&RUN solubilizes chromatin only after the targeted cleavage reaction, it should be appropriate for extending classical chromatin salt-fractionation (Sanders, 1978; Teves and Henikoff, 2012; Jahan et al., 2016) to specific TFs and chromatin complexes.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the compatibility of CUT&RUN with differential solubility, supported by the centromere data.

claims.claim: The long reach of antibody-tethered MNase can probe the local environment in intact nuclei.
claims.source: A consequence of using intact nuclei for CUT&RUN is that the long reach of antibody-tethered MNase can probe the local environment.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the observation of extended cleavage patterns and flanking nucleosomes.

claims.claim: In yeast, cleavages on one surface of the DNA flanking the TF were observed, gradually decreasing with distance.
claims.source: In yeast, we observed cleavages on one surface of the DNA flanking the TF, gradually decreasing with distance.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the 10 bp periodic cleavage pattern observed in Figure 3.

claims.claim: In human cells, cleavages at sites previously identified as contact sites for CTCF were observed.
claims.source: In human cells, we observed cleavages at sites previously identified as contact sites for CTCF.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison with ChIA-PET and Hi-C data.

claims.claim: Hi-C contact sites have been predicted computationally with a high degree of confidence given sites of CTCF binding.
claims.source: Recently, Hi-C contact sites have been predicted computationally with a high degree of confidence given sites of CTCF binding (Sanborn et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published computational study.

claims.claim: CUT&RUN can provide a complete high-resolution 1D map of a genome while enriching its 3D contact map with high-resolution distinctions between direct and indirect TF binding sites.
claims.source: As CUT&RUN maps both CTCF binding sites and interactions, and our native ChIP protocol identifies those sites that are directly TF-bound, it can provide a complete high-resolution 1D map of a genome while enriching its 3D contact map with high-resolution distinctions between direct and indirect TF binding sites.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined CUT&RUN and native ChIP data for CTCF.

claims.claim: ChIP-seq analysis typically includes normalization to compensate for different numbers of reads between samples.
claims.source: ChIP-seq analysis typically includes normalization to compensate for different numbers of reads between samples.
claims.evidence: This is based on standard practices in ChIP-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: In ChIP-seq, whole genome fragmentation leads to a constant low density genome-wide background that provides a basis for normalization.
claims.source: In ChIP-seq, whole genome fragmentation leads to a constant low density genome-wide background that provides a basis for normalization, for example, in comparing wildtype and knockdown cell lines.
claims.evidence: This is based on the principles of ChIP-seq normalization.

claims.claim: Normalization fails on abundant proteins in ChIP-seq, but this can be corrected by the use of spike-in controls.
claims.source: Although normalization fails on abundant proteins, this can be corrected by the use of spike-in controls (Bonhoure et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2015; Orlando et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies on spike-in normalization for ChIP-seq.

claims.claim: A rigorous spike-in strategy for ChIP-seq requires the addition of cells from a different species, and quantification is reliant upon antibody cross-reactivity.
claims.source: However, a rigorous spike-in strategy requires the addition of cells from a different species, and quantification is reliant upon antibody cross-reactivity (Orlando et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation describing spike-in methods for ChIP-seq.

claims.claim: Simply adding a constant low amount of fragmented spike-in DNA from a different species suffices for CUT&RUN normalization and allows accurate quantification of protein occupancy.
claims.source: To normalize between samples despite the low background in CUT&RUN, we find that simply adding a constant low amount of fragmented spike-in DNA from a different species suffices and allows accurate quantification of protein occupancy.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the spike-in normalization experiments shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: Only ~10 million paired-end reads were required for each CTCF time point, similar to the requirement for low-resolution ChIP-seq, and many fewer than for ChIP-exo, which required ~100 million reads for CTCF.
claims.source: For example only ~10 million paired-end reads were required for each CTCF time point, similar to the requirement for low-resolution ChIP-seq, and many fewer than for ChIP-exo, which required ~100 million reads for CTCF (Rhee and Pugh, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the sequencing depth comparisons and citation to ChIP-exo requirements.

claims.claim: In the cases of Max and H3K27me3, 10 million reads for CUT&RUN provided very high dynamic range, but 10 million reads were insufficient for calling peaks from Max ENCODE X-ChIP-seq.
claims.source: Furthermore, in the cases of Max and H3K27me3, 10 million reads for CUT&RUN provided very high dynamic range, but 10 million reads were insufficient for calling peaks from Max ENCODE X-ChIP-seq.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis of Max and H3K27me3 data.

claims.claim: The cost-effectiveness of CUT&RUN makes it attractive as a replacement for ChIP-seq especially where depth of sequencing is limiting.

results.result: CUT&RUN is a chromatin profiling method performed in situ where antibody-targeted MNase cleaves DNA around protein binding sites, releasing specific protein-DNA complexes into the supernatant. The method achieves limit digestion rapidly at 0°C, with fragment size distributions remaining consistent across a 32-fold time range (4-128 seconds), and supernatant extraction quantitatively recovers TF-bound fragments.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C18-C22, and C24 collectively establish the core CUT&RUN methodology with strong experimental support. The gel electrophoresis (Figure 1B), fragment size distributions (Figure 1C), and comparison of supernatant vs. total DNA extraction (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) provide direct evidence for the method's principles and quantitative recovery.

results.result: CUT&RUN yields precise transcription factor profiles in yeast with high sensitivity and specificity. For Abf1 and Reb1, >90% of TF sites show occupancy over their corresponding motifs with negligible cross-occupancy, demonstrating improved sensitivity/specificity trade-offs relative to ChIP-seq.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C25-C30 are strongly supported by motif analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), heat maps showing motif occupancy (Figure 2), and direct comparisons with ORGANIC and standard ChIP-seq. The near-complete correspondence between motif presence and TF occupancy with minimal cross-reactivity provides compelling evidence.

results.result: CUT&RUN achieves near base-pair resolution, revealing sharp 20 bp footprints for Abf1 and Reb1 centered over their motifs. The method detects 10 bp periodic cleavage patterns flanking TF binding sites, matching B-form DNA helical periodicity, suggesting tethered MNase preferentially accesses one face of the DNA helix and can cleave nearby nucleosomal DNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C35 are supported by high-resolution footprint analysis (Figure 3A) and autocorrelation analysis confirming 10 bp periodicity independent of base composition (Figure 3B). The interpretation linking periodicity to DNA structure is reasonable given the known 10 bp/turn of B-form DNA, though the mechanistic inference about chromatin flexibility (C34) is more speculative.

results.result: CUT&RUN efficiently maps large, dynamic chromatin-associated complexes including Mot1 and Sth1. Mot1 profiles obtained with ~15% the sequencing depth of ORGANIC show expected upstream positioning relative to TBP sites, while Sth1 profiles show gradual yield increases over time with negligible background in negative controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C42 are supported by comparative data for Mot1 (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and Sth1 (Figure 4B-C) showing concordance with ORGANIC profiling but with higher efficiency. The negative control for Sth1 (C40) demonstrates specificity. The conclusion about mapping large dynamic complexes (C42) is well-justified by these examples.

results.result: CUT&RUN successfully maps the rare, insoluble yeast centromeric nucleosome containing Cse4 and H2A. Both histones show maximum occupancy confined to the ~120 bp functional centromere with 4-fold better resolution than standard X-ChIP, demonstrating that CUT&RUN can map rare, insoluble, AT-rich complexes without MNase sequence bias.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C48, C50-C52 are strongly supported by centromere mapping data (Figure 5A-C) showing co-localization of Cse4 and H2A at all 16 yeast centromeres. The demonstration of H2A in the centromeric nucleosome (C50) addresses a controversy with appropriate citations. The lack of AT-bias (C51) is convincingly shown given the >90% A+T content of centromeric DNA.

results.result: Analysis of ≥150 bp fragments reveals broad peaks around TF binding sites extending ~0.5 kb on either side, with 'notches' at the sites themselves that deepen with digestion time. This extended cleavage pattern suggests the flexibility of the antibody-MNase tether allows probing of nearby chromatin.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 are supported by ≥150 bp fragment profiles (Figures 1D, 2, 4) and heat map analysis showing extended occupancy. The interpretation (C54, C56) that this represents gradual release of fragments with one end near the TF and flexibility of the tether is reasonable, though somewhat speculative. The comparison to DamID's >1 kb reach (C56) provides useful context.

results.result: CUT&RUN maps human CTCF at high resolution with higher dynamic range than X-ChIP-seq and ChIP-exo when comparing 10 million reads. The method shows undetectable background in no-antibody controls, reveals pronounced 'tram-tracks' separated by 44 bp with consistent cleavage patterns over a ~300-fold time range, and maps both TFs and flanking nucleosomes simultaneously.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C64 are well-supported by CTCF mapping data (Figure 6A-C) showing superior dynamic range, negative controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), and precise cleavage patterns. The consistency of cleavage over time (C62) and the interpretation of homogeneous positioning (C63) are supported by the data, though the exact biological meaning requires some inference.

results.result: CUT&RUN successfully mapped Myc and Max at high resolution, with Max CUT&RUN showing much higher dynamic range than ENCODE ChIP-seq and identifying a much larger number of Max binding sites. Max is present at almost all Myc sites as expected, while ENCODE X-ChIP-seq identified 10-fold fewer Max sites despite showing high occupancy when aligned to Max CUT&RUN sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C69 are supported by Myc/Max mapping data (Figure 6—figure supplement 3). The comparison with ENCODE data (C66, C68-C69) demonstrates CUT&RUN's superior sensitivity, with the heat map analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C) showing that X-ChIP-seq signal is present but below detection threshold. The Myc-Max overlap (C67) validates expected biology.

results.result: CUT&RUN maps H3K27me3 in compacted heterochromatin with similar landscapes but much higher dynamic range compared to ENCODE X-ChIP-seq. H3K27me3-marked chromatin is readily released into the soluble fraction, demonstrating that Protein A-MNase can access compacted chromatin.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72 are supported by H3K27me3 mapping data (Figure 6—figure supplement 4) showing successful profiling of this repressive mark. The inference that pA-MN can access compacted chromatin (C71-C72) is reasonable given H3K27me3's association with heterochromatin, though direct structural evidence is not provided.

results.result: By combining CUT&RUN with native ChIP, direct and indirect CTCF binding sites can be distinguished at near base-pair resolution. Native ChIP identified 2,298 high-motif-score sites while CUT&RUN detected ~22,000 sites. CUT&RUN-only sites show footprints in native ChIP input and correlate with ChIA-PET and Hi-C contact sites, enabling directional mapping of long-range genomic interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C81 are supported by native ChIP development (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), comparative analysis (Figure 7A-B), and validation with ChIA-PET (Figure 8A, C) and Hi-C data (Figure 8B). The distinction between direct and indirect sites is well-established, with 91% of direct sites present in ChIA-PET data and quantitative correlation between Hi-C scores and CUT&RUN signal at indirect sites.

results.result: CUT&RUN allows quantitative measurements with low cell numbers. When normalized to spike-in DNA, cleavage events are proportional to starting cell number, while standard normalization shows no clear differences between samples, suggesting high data quality is maintained with low input material.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83 are supported by cell titration experiments (Figure 9) showing proportional response with spike-in normalization and consistent quality with standard normalization. The data demonstrate both quantitative accuracy and robustness across different cell numbers (600,000 to 10 million cells).

results.result: CUT&RUN is simple, robust, and requires only ~1/10th the sequencing depth of ChIP-seq due to intrinsically low background from in situ targeted cleavage. The method requires ~10 million paired-end reads for CTCF (similar to low-resolution ChIP-seq but far fewer than ChIP-exo's ~100 million), making it cost-effective for transcription factor profiling.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C84-C85, C92, C106-C108 are supported by consistent comparisons throughout showing 2-3 million reads for yeast TFs versus 20-30 million for ORGANIC, and ~10 million for human CTCF versus ~100 million for ChIP-exo. The mechanistic explanation (C92) that targeted cleavage reduces background is logical and supported by negative controls.

results.result: Because nuclei remain intact during MNase activation, CUT&RUN can probe the local chromatin environment around targeted sites. The method recovers 3D contact sites with base-pair resolution, observing cleavages on one DNA face flanking yeast TFs and at previously identified CTCF contact sites in human cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87, C96-C98 are supported by observations of flanking nucleosomes, extended cleavage patterns (Figure 3), and validation with ChIA-PET/Hi-C data (Figure 8). The ability to probe local environment is demonstrated, though the mechanistic details of how 3D contacts lead to cleavage require some inference.

results.result: CUT&RUN is antibody-based and widely applicable to any chromatin epitope, providing quantitative occupancy profiles with standard and spike-in normalization options. The only non-standard requirement is pA-MN fusion protein, which can be produced in sufficient quantities for >100,000 samples from a single bacterial culture batch.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90, C105 are supported by successful application to multiple targets (histones, TFs, histone modifications) and spike-in normalization experiments (Figure 9). The calculation for pA-MN yield (C90) is based on the protocol but not directly validated experimentally. The spike-in strategy (C105) is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: CUT&RUN resolves crosslinking-, sonication-, and solubilization-related issues inherent to ChIP because it operates on different principles. The method shows near absence of background under brief low-temperature conditions, lacks preference for accessible or AT-rich DNA, and achieves zero-order cleavage kinetics with steady particle release.
results.evaluation: Claims C91, C93, C109-C110 are supported by the in situ nature of the method, recovery of essentially all Abf1/Reb1 motifs, successful mapping of AT-rich centromeres, and consistent cleavage across time points. The mechanistic explanations (C109-C110) are reasonable inferences from the data, though some aspects are speculative.

results.result: Accounting for epitope abundances, mapping ~22,000 CTCF sites with 600,000 cells is comparable in sensitivity to ultra-low input ChIP-seq protocols that map abundant histone modifications with ~5,000 cells. However, ultra-low-input ChIP provides only ~2 kb resolution while CUT&RUN provides near base-pair resolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C112 are supported by the demonstrated cell number requirements and resolution comparisons. The sensitivity comparison (C111) requires accounting for the ~100-fold difference in epitope abundance between CTCF and H3K27me3, which is reasonable but involves some estimation. The resolution advantage is clearly demonstrated throughout.

results.result: CUT&RUN has practical advantages including antibody binding in intact nuclear environment (potentially successful with antibodies validated cytologically), compatibility with salt-fractionation, suitability for automation, and potential application to epigenome diagnostics. The method is an attractive alternative to ChIP-seq.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95, C113-C115 include speculative statements about future applications and potential advantages. While C94-C95 and C113 are reasonable extrapolations marked as speculation/inference, they lack direct experimental validation. The summary statements (C114-C115) are supported by the overall body of work but represent conclusions rather than specific testable results.

results.result: Background on existing methods: ChIP has changed little since 1985; crosslinking causes epitope masking and false positives; native ChIP provides direct protein-DNA interaction maps but has extraction efficiency issues; DamID resolution is limited by GATC site distribution; ChEC-seq achieved near base-pair resolution; enzyme tethering methods require fusion constructs for each target.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C17 provide background context supported by appropriate citations to published literature. These are primarily literature review claims establishing the rationale for developing CUT&RUN, accurately representing prior work based on the citations provided.

results.result: Background on normalization and 3D genome mapping: Hi-C contact sites can be computationally predicted from CTCF binding; ChIP-seq normalization typically uses genome-wide background but fails for abundant proteins; spike-in controls can correct this but require cross-species cells and antibody cross-reactivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C104 provide background on normalization strategies and 3D genome methods, supported by appropriate citations. These accurately represent standard practices and published methods, providing context for CUT&RUN's spike-in normalization approach.

results.result: Structural information: Abf1 has two DNA-binding domains spaced ~10 bp apart while Reb1 has a single Myb-like DNA-binding domain.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C117 are factual statements about TF structure supported by citations to published structural studies. These provide relevant context for interpreting the footprinting results.
